## The question

[How can I find the volume enclosed by the following graphs?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2005581/how-can-i-find-the-volume-enclosed-by-the-following-graphs), asked by [Reed Oei](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/113879/reed-oei) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2016-11-08; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> How do I find the volume bound by planes $x=0$, $y=0$, and the surfaces $x=-4y^2+3$, $z=x^3y$?
>
> I think that I probably need to do:
>
> $$\iint_D (x^3y) \, dx\,dy$$
>
> But I'm not sure what to do for the limits. I think that for the $x$ I should use $0$ and $-4y^2+3$, but I don't know what to do about the $y$.
>
> EDIT: I tried using 0 and 3 for the limits for $x$, and $0$ and $\frac{\sqrt{3-x}}{2}$ as limits for the $y$, but I got half of the answer that I was supposed to get ($\frac{243}{80}$).
:::

Alternatively to Behrouz's answer, the solid lies over the plane region
$$D = \left\{(x,y)\mid - \sqrt{3}/2 \leq y \leq \sqrt{3}/2,\ 0 \leq x \leq -4y^2+3\right\}$$
[It looks like this][1]:

[![set][2]][2]

So the volume is
$$\int_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2} \int_0^{3-4y^2} x^3y\,dx\,dy$$


  [1]: http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?t=crmtb01&f=ob&i=x%20%E2%89%A50%20and%20x%20%E2%89%A4-4y%5E2%20%2B%203
